utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As usual, good afternoon, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I hear and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to be patient. I have to put the same question every day. So it's not a question because I doubt whether you get interpretation, but I need to put the same question every day just to make sure that the interpretation is okay. Not to bother you, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. General Talic, good afternoon to you. And I put the same question to you: Can you understand me in a language -- can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. My name is Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecution with the case manager, Denise Gustin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm Milka Maglov, a lawyer, and the lead counsel, Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. I represent General Talic together with colleague Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness? Okay. Usher, could you please bring the witness. And we'll go into closed session, please, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think perhaps I can get started while the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, can I take up the matter that Mr. Cayley referred to at the end of the last session, and that is, I'm afraid, the problems that are caused as far as particularly my attendance is going to be in this case next week. Your Honour, the Stakic case, notwithstanding our attempts to persuade Judge Schomburg that it should be delayed, is going to start next Tuesday. The case will be opened -- or the opening will certainly commence on Tuesday morning. Your Honour, I don't think it's going to cause a problem, because I think the next -- there are three witnesses now to come who are what we've called crime-based witnesses. And I think that will probably take tomorrow, Monday, and Tuesday. But it may be that the -- they do finish early on Tuesday. I've got to call the witness who follows on who's Witness number 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was a change of switch yesterday. I just want to make sure that we've got the names -- not the names, the numbers right. Just to confirm it with you, Ms. Korner. That's all. This is Witness 7.171. Yes, BT12 is Witness 7.171. And then there was a switch, as I was informed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness after him will be 7.160.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then 7.197.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then let's leave 7.4, because I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's the one that I'm going to be calling. And it may be that he could start on Tuesday afternoon, and I'm asking for Your Honours' indulgence not to have to call him until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That shouldn't be a problem with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to 7.4?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it right. So basically we're talking of this witness plus another two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And presumably ready by Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, then after those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you're asking to produce 7.4 Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay with us, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, and it may be that any remaining time can be filled in by that excellent exercise so enjoyed by Mr. Ackerman of having a look at some more documents, because we haven't actually looked at some of the document Volume 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the exercise he will rise and ask that his own documents will be read too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Anyhow, Your Honour, that's the first matter. And I do apologise. It shouldn't happen too often, but it is next week a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I mean, you have the understanding of this Tribunal. And I know that you -- the same Prosecution team in this case is the Prosecution team in the other case. So I appreciate the problems that -- the difficulties that you have to face.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I say, I hope it won't be too -- Mr. Cayley normally will not be involved in the Stakic case but has to deal with one Dr. Donia yet again in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem, Ms. Korner. I mean, you will find this Court cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not just you, but also the Defence, as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that, however, brings me to an allied problem, which is this question of the crossover of the witnesses. Now, Your Honour hasn't given a ruling yet on the motion for depositions, but it was discussed yesterday in the Pre-Trial Conference, and it's perfectly apparent that because of the divergence in the evidence at the moment between the two cases -- in fact, because we're nowhere near Prijedor, that the logistics are going to make this suggested course just unworkable. And I understand from what Judge Schomburg said, that you and he had in fact discussed the matter. But Your Honour, there is coming in the Stakic trial a witness. The disclosure number of which in this trial is 7.35. I would be very grateful if the Defence in this case could have a look at the transcript that they have been given. He has testified before. We would wish to tender him in this case under Rule 92, but it may be that they will feel that he is someone that they wish to cross-examine. If that is right, although it would interrupt the Sanski Most evidence, we would wish to him -- to tender him in this case the week after next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Korner. Given the order of witnesses that you intend to present in the Sanski Most municipality, where does -- because I don't have that in front of me -- where does this particular witness fit in?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He comes from Prijedor. But that's the whole point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With a great deal of reluctance -- but we are enormously concerned about this business of witnesses coming and going. We would like to interrupt Sanski Most and interpose, if the Defence require to cross-examine him, this particular witness. As I say, he's got the disclosure number 7.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I read you now. I wasn't reading you 100 per cent before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for a decision today, but I'm merely asking Your Honours and the Defence to perhaps consider that matter over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this would entail how long a stoppage in the Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it would really depend -- we would propose to -- he would be called in the Stakic case on Thursday and Friday of next week. We would then provide to the Defence in this case the transcript of what he said in the Stakic case and ask to interpose him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The date would be -- today is the 11th, plus seven, 18th and 19th --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He would be called in the Stakic case on 18th and 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of April. Mm-hm. And you propose to hand to the Defence the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The rough version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Roughly that of the 18th on the 19th and that of the 19th, I would suppose, on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Interpose him if we have to on the Wednesday, because we're not sitting on the 23rd because of a plenary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Well, that's a foregone conclusion on your part. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've discussed it a little bit, and it's not to be excluded that I -- I informed the President of the ICTY that I think I should have the sitting nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that would be very helpful, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I will of course inform you beforehand. But don't take it for granted that because there is a plenary on the 23rd, that means that definitely we are not sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, well, I hadn't appreciated that, Your Honour. So we'd be very grateful if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I had it in mind -- I have discussed it already with others, and I still have to discuss it with my two colleagues and then come to a decision. But you will know in good time what's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. I mean, it would be very helpful, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the understanding, Ms. Korner, is that if any one of us three prefers to be present at the plenary, which takes precedence, actually, over the sitting, then obviously the sitting will not take place on the 23rd. Otherwise, we will hold the sitting, and we will explain to the President that between what's being discussed between 2.15 and 6.30 in the plenary and here, we have opted for this. But you will be informed in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, may I simply say, Your Honour, with the added complication of this particular witness, we -- the first witness in Sanski Most is 7.77. It would be nice to be able to finish him off within the week, because otherwise we have a week off and he has to come back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 77. He's the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, if you let us have his statements in good time --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we would be able to make an assessment of how long -- and then if needs be, we can direct you and Defence teams as to what to concentrate upon during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination so that we will condense everything, what is relevant, because so far I've -- we have allowed you a lot of room and a lot of space. But we may have to cut down on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this may be a good reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we can let Your Honours have it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not just us, but also the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They've got them. They've got all the statements. Your Honour, that's -- those -- that's one of the two matters that I had to mention -- sorry, one of the three. The second matter is this. And I've mentioned it mainly to Madam Fauveau because it affects her more than anybody else. Coming from Sanski Most is a witness who was one of the few survivors of a massacre in the garage. There's her and her sister. The sister has been accepted by the Defence under Rule 92, although Your Honours have still got to make a ruling. But it's one of the ones that was accepted. But that was on the basis that one of the two sisters was going to attend. Neither -- well, effectively, neither sister, who were both very young at the time -- one was 16 and the other was 11 -- will -- at the moment they're both refusing to attend because they're saying they cannot bear to relive these matters, although they did sign statements saying they would attend. I'm raising it, Your Honour, and I've raised it be Madam Fauveau, who as I say, it affects most of all, because I'm going to ask if it could be considered whether these women really have to attend, either of them. I can and I will, if I'm told that they must attend -- I would have to apply for a witness summons for the sister that we listed to attend. But I'm telling Your Honours this, and I've raised it, as I say, with Madam Fauveau, in the hopes that perhaps some arrangement or agreement can become available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Short of that, Ms. Korner, what's the other alternative that you may be ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only alternative is to apply to Your Honours for a witness summons which will be served upon her and she will be told that she must attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This witness has never given evidence in any other trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I don't know whether you were prepared for this. If you were, perhaps you could illuminate the Chamber. If you are not, of course, you can come back to the Chamber at an adequate time and let us know what the position of General Talic is in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I spoke to Ms. Korner, and I asked her if I can give my reply on Monday. Having said that, I do have empathy with this young woman, but it seems that there are no other witnesses who are speaking about the same event. So I will see what I can do. And if we can make an arrangement to avoid the young woman coming here. But I have to say I have much reserve on this possibility, that I would actually accept this 92 bis Rule, but I promise that I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no other -- there's one other witness who's coming, but he didn't actually see the killings. He's going to talk about the discovery of the bodies. But it is only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same incident, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the same incident, but only these two -- it's only these two sisters who provided statements -- I'm sorry, there was one relation to the family, but she was 80, and it was impossible. There was just no way we could deal with her. So effectively, we're in that position. Your Honour, that really, I think, deals with -- and I'm sorry to have raised all these witness problems at this late stage, particularly with the witness sitting here waiting to start. The final matter is this: I understand from what I was told that I certainly misled the Chamber and Mr. Ackerman when I said that the witness about whom we had all this discussion earlier this week had asked for protective measures. I understood that to be taken as had asked us to apply for. Obviously we haven't been applying for all witnesses. We've been doing it municipality by municipality. We're now going to put in a motion to cover everybody so that that situation doesn't arise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, I'm sorry that the Court was misled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These things happen, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understood what I meant, but I obviously didn't make it clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that means we can start with you, sir. Welcome -- I think he needs to put -- Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't realise you did not have the headphones on before. I thought you were following the discussion. The discussion actually had nothing to do with you. Otherwise, of course, we -- I would give orders to have it started again. This was organisational matters that we were discussing. I am sorry you had to wait for all these minutes until we could get started with your evidence. I didn't realise it was going to take this long. I was assured before I started that it was only a question of a couple of minutes. Again, once more, good afternoon, and welcome to this Trial Chamber. The Chamber is very grateful that you have come over to give your testimony. The gentleman sitting -- standing next to you is now going to hand you a piece of paper, on which there is a statement -- a solemn declaration that you are kindly asked to make. But before you make it -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I would ask the Court if the declaration could be read to the witness and if he could repeat it back. He has some poor eyesight and prefers to have things read to him rather than read it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read B/C/S? Because it's -- I think what we need to do is you read in English and the interpreter will interpret -- will interpret -- will translate. And the witness, as soon as you hear the interpreter translating the statement in your own language, please, there will be a pause, and you are kindly asked to repeat the same words in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So please read slowly sentence by sentence. I know there isn't much, but we'll go bit by bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see? We have found a solution. You may now sit down. And I will now explain to you -- the gentleman can now sit down. And I will try to explain to you very briefly the procedure of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not know if you have ever been in a Tribunal like this. I know from your statement that you have been in a court of law. This is a little bit different. You are in an International Tribunal. We are the three Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am the Presiding Judge, and I have two other Judges sitting with me to hear and determine this case, a case which has been brought by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against two persons. One person is Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, and the other person is General Talic, Momir Talic. Now, if you look to your right, you see three persons near you. And that's the team for the Prosecution. Now, you will not necessarily see the same faces every day. Those faces may change. But those three persons represent the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. And they will be the first to go ahead with what you are here for, and that is answering a set of questions. The Prosecution will put to you some questions. There will be quite a few of them, I would imagine. And your duty here is to keep calm and try to answer those questions, all the questions. Don't tell us more than you are asked and don't tell us less than you are asked. So you answer the question, the whole question, and possibly nothing but the question. Having finished that stage, there will be two other teams of lawyers. The first team is -- if you look on your left, you see again three persons in the front row, and that's the -- on the front row, that's the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin. And behind them, there is -- there are two persons, and that's the Defence team for General Talic, behind the first row in the back, behind you, there is the Defence -- the other Defence team. They have a right under the law of this Tribunal to question you as well. It's not just the Prosecution that puts questions to you but also the Defence. That's something which is fundamentally important in the proceedings of this Tribunal. I know that the evidence you are going to give here, sir, are events which may not be easy for you to give evidence upon, at least according to what I read from your previous statement to the Prosecution. You have to understand that the Prosecution, ourselves, the Defence, and you are on the same journey. We have the same interest. And that is establishing the truth. Therefore, you have to keep calm, and you -- although it may not be easy, you have to do your best not to let yourself be carried away emotionally. I am now going to ask Ms. Korner -- you will be conducting the examination-in-chief, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, Mr. Nicholls will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, okay. I'm now going to ask Mr. Nicholls to stand up and commence his examination-in-chief. Before he does, is there anything you would like to state -- to ask this Chamber? Have you understood what I have tried to explain to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To begin with, I would ask if we could go into private session for some of the initial material which could otherwise potentially identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll go into open session now, please. Okay. We are in public session now. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said the relations were good. Did you have -- were you friends with Serbs and Croats, as well as with other Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I understand you were -- briefly you did a brief two-year military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after that, you were in the reserves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During this time, the whole time you lived in your village, were you involved in any political activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you interested in politics? That is, did you follow politics in newspapers, on television, or on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What type of work did you do? Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I was a farmer, and I was also employed in a company in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the name of that company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: It was the utility company [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was a large company which employed a great many people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you stop working for that utility company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Somewhere at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you come to stop working for the utility company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, we didn't want to partake in the Serbian army, and we were dismissed and that they would call us later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "we," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: We, the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were all of the Muslims and Croats dismissed from the company in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Those who joined their army, no. But those who didn't want to join their army had to leave the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was it that actually told you that you were dismissed from this sanitation -- or from this utility company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, it -- the management told us that we were redundant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were any workers of Serb ethnicity dismissed from the company at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, those who didn't -- if they didn't want to join their army, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls, because Ms. Fauveau -- Madam Fauveau has got -- no. You almost had visitors, Madam Fauveau. I think you still have.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's okay. We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Once you were dismissed from the company in late 1991, what did you do next to support yourself and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, I was farming. I worked on the farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was your house located -- your home located on the same farm that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move ahead a little bit and talk about some of the -- ask you some questions about some of the military operations which you were able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have the map. If this could be placed on the ELMO. Sorry, I don't know -- the Defence -- you don't have copies of -- Okay. Could you pass these out to the Defence counsel and the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at that map for a moment and tell us whether that map is a fair and an accurate representation of the area which it depicts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, [redacted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And from that hill, you could see much of this surrounding area which you see before you on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at sometime, did you begin to see tanks appearing in this area? If you could tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you first see a tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I saw it in 1991 or maybe it was 1992, anyway, before I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my question was: Which town -- you don't necessarily need to point to it -- but which town did you first see tanks appearing in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: In Balte, the first tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is that a Serb or a Muslim or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where was that tank directed towards? Which villages was it, if you could tell, aimed toward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Bastasi and Mehovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what is the predominant ethnicity of those villages which you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: More Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask that again. I'm not sure you understood. The tank at Balte was aimed at which villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Towards Culumi, Mehovci. And those are Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see that tank open fire at any point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see any other tanks appear in this region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: A tank on -- in Memici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where was that tank directed towards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Mehovci and Bastasi. They could target either of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see that tank open fire at any point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where else did you see tanks during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Near Tisovac towards Hadrovci. I saw two tanks. I saw some soldier, some men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Hadrovci is -- what is the predominant ethnicity of this town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did those tanks in Tisovac open fire at any point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure the answer was recorded. Did those tanks at Tisovac open fire? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Towards -- fire was opened towards Hadrovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what else did you see at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I could see that when I was in Bastasi and after -- up to the time I was evicted from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But did you see any damage [Realtime transcript read in error "camouflage"] occurring from that shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I saw the houses burning. One could see it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many houses you saw burning as a result of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't say "camouflage," I believe, in the transcript, if that can be corrected. And the village where you saw those houses burning, were those Muslim houses or Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Houses of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you see any other of the villages in that area shelled during this period or attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't -- hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask. Do you recall an attack -- any attacks originating from Popovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is that -- was Popovac a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which villages -- or where did you see -- what was the object which villages were attacked from Popovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Vranic and Basici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able to see whether any damage -- could you describe those attacks, any damage you were able to see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: We could see houses burning. And once the shell falls, it -- the houses were ignited and started burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall seeing any attack from Popovac on Mehovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, certainly they attacked. I didn't see it myself, but I saw the houses burning and the people fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean you saw the people fleeing? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, they were fleeing from the shelling. They were fleeing through my village in order to save their necks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I know you don't know the exact day, but if you could give me an approximate time when this shelling occurred and when you saw these people fleeing through your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: It was approximately two or one. They went through this village. They were my relatives. Others went by another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And my question is: Do you remember approximately what month this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: It was prior to the month of August. Maybe June or July, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during these attacks which you have described, this shelling, at any point did you see any kind of return fire from the Muslim villages which were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: They didn't have the weapons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But did you see any form of resistance to these attacks by the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, all these attacks which you've described originated from Serb villages and were targeted at Muslim villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that they didn't -- people didn't have any weapons to resist these attacks. Are you aware, did the Muslim population in this area have any weapons? Did anybody that you know of have any rifles, hunting rifles, pistols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, they had hunting rifles and pistols with a permit, but prior to that they already came and collected these weapons in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who collected these weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Civil police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And these were collected from the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes. And they also said that they would return these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were the weapons ever returned, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No, no. There's nobody there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell me, during this time period, late 1991 into 1992, did the Serbian population of this area have their weapons taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No. They were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How were you aware of that, what you've just said, that they were -- that the Serbian population was actually given weapons and that their weapons were not taken away? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: At the Milinkovic's house, they were bringing them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What do you mean by that? You saw weapons being brought in at this particular house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I went to Karanovac. I passed that building. I saw a truck full of weapons. I was -- it wasn't clear to me whether they were unloading the truck or loading it. I didn't even dare stop by and watch. I just passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But then was it common knowledge, or how did you know that your Serb neighbours had weapons but that your Muslim neighbours did not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would -- I don't like this question at all, Mr. Nicholls. Could you rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could ask you again, how were you aware or what was your basis of knowing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think the question to ask to the witness is whether his -- what he saw in Karanovac, what he's just explained, the loading or unloading, could not be exactly precise on that, on weapons on or from a truck was the only basis or information he has on the basis of which he can say that the Serbs were given arms rather than have weapons taken away from them or whether he had other information, other bases for his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Other than that incident that you've described, do you have any other basis for your information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, neighbours came to see me, all Serbs, and they all had weapons. Even a child who would be 15 years old, and even a child of 15 would be bearing a rifle, a long rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, going back to the incidents of shelling which you described. What effect did that have on the Muslim population in your area and in your town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Nobody was able to sleep. Everyone was afraid of shells. And the Serbs told us that we mustn't move in groups, that they would kill us. So we had to escape. We wouldn't dare stay in the house. We saw houses burn in Hadrovci in Memic. We saw these houses burn in neighbouring hamlets. So I had to hide. I had to go into the fields, into the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say that, do you mean that you left your home and you stayed in the woods? Could you explain that a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I never stayed in my house at night. I was always outside, because I was afraid of shells or whether they would come and slit our throats. I was constantly afraid of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And would your whole family leave the house at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes. Only the people who are old, who couldn't leave the houses, then they stayed. Some neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did there come a time where you tried to take other steps to protect yourself and your family? Did you ever try to leave the area because of this shelling which you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me about that. Where did you try to go? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Well, I had set off to escape into the town. I thought I would feel freer in the town. So I got to Karanovac and the Serb army wouldn't let me get through, so they told me to go back. They said, "There's more of your people, so go out there. You can see them sitting outside." And there were two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for a moment. Where were you trying to get to when you left? What village or place were you trying to reach?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I tried to go to Novoselija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And without saying their names, what members of your family -- or who accompanied you when you tried to move, to go to Novoselija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: My wife and my daughter-in-law and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What were you able to bring with you at this time when you were trying to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Only what I had on me. So I just got into the cart drawn by a horse and set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how far is Novoselija from -- well, that's not important. You said that you reached Karanovac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And please tell the Chamber -- you were starting to -- what happened when you reached Karanovac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I got to the checkpoint, and then they asked me where I was going. I said I was going to Novoselija. And then they told me, "You can't go through. Go back. Go back to Svrakava. There are your people there, more of your people there."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Who was manning this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I don't know. They were in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I think you said earlier it was an army checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes. There were soldiers in camouflage. They were armed. You couldn't recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you recognise in particular any insignia on these camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No, I didn't even look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did you do when you were told that you were not allowed to proceed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: They ordered immediately that these two soldiers should take me up to these people who were gathered in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was that field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: It was a field near Karanovac called Svrakava. That's near Jasinj Dvor [phoen]. It was a field. There was a field there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said "the people" in that field. Who was in that field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: There were -- there were people who were from Basici, and there were people who were stopped there and told to be in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the people in that field from Basici, were those soldiers or civilians? What type of people were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: Civilians. They were all Muslims. Women, children, people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was anybody guarding them in this field? Were they free to leave? Can you just describe a setting a little bit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: No. There was the army there, the soldiers, and the police from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you can tell me approximately how many civilians were being -- were being kept or were in that field.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: At least 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how did you and your wife -- what happened next? How did you come to leave the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: We were told to go there, and then -- then I wanted to ask who was the senior officer so that I could ask. And there was police as well. So I went to one of them, one policeman. I recognised him. And there was some civilians. And then they told me, "What are you doing here?" So I said, "I had set off to go to Novoselija and they wouldn't let me go through and they returned me."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: And then they told me, "Who have you got of your family there?" So I said, "I've got my wife and y daughter-in-law, and I've got a cart with a horse." And he said, "You take your own and go back, go back home."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to those people in the field? Did you personally ever see those people again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I saw that they were moved out to Karanovac to a school or in front of the school. It's a school which had a fence around, and I saw them there for two or three days, and I didn't see them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after you returned to your home, what did you do then? Did you carry on living there at that time, or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT12
utterances.text: I continued to live there until this happened. I was just doing the -- the work on the farm. And when this happened, of course I had to leave everything and flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd request that we return to private session now for the next area of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That these killings had occurred in the way in which the witness's statement said that they had. And I learned a moment ago that Ms. Fauveau had done the same, and that was done in an effort to keep the witnesses from having to go through what this gentleman just went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there apparently has been some miscommunication or something -- and I don't know what happened. But I didn't want to raise it in the middle of the testimony, because I thought it might distress him even further. But that's what we did, and we were trying to prevent the trauma that I think this witness just experienced -- to some extent reexperienced. And apparently it didn't work. But with regard to cross-examination, I will have no questions of this witness unless there's some testimony that I haven't heard yet that would prompt me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will have about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So more or less --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- Madam Fauveau I certainly recollect giving me a letter saying that they didn't contest the murders. There's a contest over this business of Serb soldiers, which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is obvious, yes. To be expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have absolutely no recollection of receiving anything from Mr. Ackerman. I may be wrong -- in writing or verbally on this witness, save for a communication sometime ago which I was instructed to keep private and certainly didn't specify any particular witnesses. And so on this particular witness, I have no recollection at all of him saying that there was no contest whatsoever from the Defence and we needn't call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is referring to exactly the letter that I was referring to. What I did with that letter, rather than witnesses, was I went through the -- the indictment and said to Ms. Korner that I do not contest the evidence regarding these killings. And I listed them all, as I recall -- in the indictment. And what I -- the reason I asked her -- I asked her not to inform the Trial Chamber of that unless the same kind of a -- an offer was forthcoming from Ms. Fauveau because I didn't want it to appear that I was trying to curry the favour of the Trial Chamber and make General Talic's team look like they were being unfair. And that's the reason I did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think that was an appropriate thing for me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you're not being criticised by anyone, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he is. I am. I'm sorry, Your Honour. That's absolutely no good, giving me a letter saying, "I don't want you to let anybody know unless a public statement is made to that effect, I can't go on the basis of a private communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. The position is better late than never, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we had better be informed in terms in open court or in an open public document what is not disputed, by both counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you need to take this up. We have to stop, because I owe it to the interpreters to stop at 6.30 sharp. But I think you need to address this between now and tomorrow morning, particularly since the next one or two witnesses are crime-based too. So if we can avoid unnecessary --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not quite the same extent. The next witness is not going to talk about murders. It's more sackings and the like. But this is going to happen, Your Honour. And it's one of the reasons, of course, I raised the Sanski Most witness today. There are a lot of people who at the moment are being asked to come who are simply going to talk about atrocious killings without implicating either defendant directly. And so we do want to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If these witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A hundred per cent right. And not just you want to know, but we are very much interested in knowing that too, because it's our duty to mitigate -- lessen the traumas people have to go through in this Tribunal. It's no fun. It's tragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I tried very hard. My intention is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But maybe I'm not criticising you, as I said, Mr. Ackerman, for not having tried. It's -- maybe the way it has been done has not been exactly the way to go about it. If there's a little bit of patching up that needs to be done, please do it between now and whenever is appropriate so that we possibly can avoid a repetition of what has happened today. I mean, it's traumatic for the witness; I suppose also for you; and for the Prosecution, as well as for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will bring you a copy of my letter. I think it was quite clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm more interested than the letter is interested in a sort of arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On a permanent or on a regular basis to be reached with the Prosecution. I thank the interpreters for their patience. I suppose they are on that side, because it's too dark. I can't see anything. I thank you for having stayed with us a little bit more than we should have. Thank you. Tomorrow afternoon at 2.15, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.32 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of April, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
